## What it does

`gseamod` tests whether a gene set is enriched for differential expression between two classes,
built from the five modules of Ackermann and Strimmer (2009): a gene-level statistic, an optional
transformation, a gene set statistic and a significance assessment, plus the global tracks
(globaltest and Hotelling's T-squared with a shrinkage correlation). The paper's recommendation
is the mean of the squared moderated t statistics, with gene sampling or sample label
permutation.

Ackermann M, Strimmer K. A general modular framework for gene set enrichment analysis.
*BMC Bioinformatics* 10:47 (2009). doi:10.1186/1471-2105-10-47. The authors' R code is lost;
this package was rebuilt from the paper's text in the
[fossil](https://github.com/jeonglab-bcm/fossil) repository.

## Install

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("jeonglab-bcm/fossil/PMC2661051/package")
```

```{r load}
library(gseamod)
packageVersion("gseamod")
```

## Example input

One data set of the paper's simulation study: 600 genes by 20 samples, two classes of 10, and
nine gene sets of 20 genes each.

```{r input}
X <- as.matrix(read.csv(example_path("sim_expression.csv"), row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE))
y <- read.csv(example_path("sim_labels.csv"))$class
sets <- read_gmt(example_path("sim_sets.gmt"))
dim(X)
X[1:3, 1:5]
table(y)
lengths(sets)
```

Sets 1 and 2 are shifted up by 0.75 (set 1 with correlation 0.6), sets 6 and 7 hold 10 genes
shifted up and 10 down by 1, sets 4, 5, 8 and 9 mix half of such genes with background genes, and
set 3 is 20 background genes (no effect).

## Run the method

The recommended combination, with both significance assessments:

```{r run}
q1 <- gsea(X, y, sets, gene = "modt", transform = "square", setstat = "mean",
           method = "resampling", B = 1000, seed = 1)
q2 <- gsea(X, y, sets, gene = "modt", transform = "square", setstat = "mean",
           method = "permutation", B = 1000, seed = 1)
data.frame(set = q1$set, statistic = round(q1$statistic, 3), p_resampling = q1$p, p_permutation = q2$p)
```

Without the squaring, the sets with genes shifted both ways (6 to 9) are missed:

```{r untransformed}
gsea(X, y, sets, transform = "none", setstat = "mean", method = "resampling", B = 1000, seed = 1)$p
```

The global and multivariate tracks:

```{r global}
gsea(X, y, sets, setstat = "hotelling", method = "permutation", B = 200, seed = 1)$p
```

## Compare with the expected output

The paper reports, for 100 simulated data sets, the share in which each set was significant at
p <= 0.05 (Table 4, resampling column). We simulate 100 data sets with `simulate_ackermann()`
and compare our shares with the printed ones within Monte Carlo error (`rate_tolerance()`, a 99%
band for two shares of 100).

```{r compare}
expected <- read.csv(example_path("paper_table4_resampling.csv"), colClasses = "character")
p <- t(vapply(1:100, function(r) {
  d <- simulate_ackermann(seed = 2009 + r)
  gsea(d$X, d$y, d$sets, gene = "modt", transform = "square", setstat = "mean",
       method = "resampling", B = 1000, seed = r)$p
}, numeric(9)))
colnames(p) <- paste0("set", 1:9)
ours <- detection_rates(p)
cmp <- data.frame(set = expected$set, paper = expected$detection_rate, ours = ours[expected$set],
                  tolerance = round(rate_tolerance(expected$detection_rate, ours[expected$set]), 3))
cmp$agrees <- abs(as.numeric(cmp$paper) - cmp$ours) <= cmp$tolerance
cmp
cat(sum(cmp$agrees), "of", nrow(cmp), "sets agree with Table 4 of the paper\n")
stopifnot(all(cmp$agrees))
```

```{r plot}
barplot(rbind(as.numeric(cmp$paper), cmp$ours), beside = TRUE, names.arg = cmp$set,
        col = c("grey30", "steelblue"), ylim = c(0, 1), ylab = "share of p <= 0.05",
        legend.text = c("paper", "gseamod"), args.legend = list(x = "topleft", bty = "n"))
```

## Your own data

- `X`: a numeric matrix with genes in rows and samples in columns, on a log scale; row names are
  gene identifiers. `read_gct()` reads GSEA's GCT files.
- `y`: one 0/1 label per column (`read_cls()` reads GSEA's CLS files; convert its labels with
  `as.numeric(cls == "MUT")` or similar).
- `sets`: a named list of gene sets, as row names or row indices (`read_gmt()` reads GMT files).
  Genes not in `X` are dropped.

Options that matter: `gene` (`"modt"`, `"t"`, `"corr"`), `transform` (`"square"`, `"none"`,
`"ranksq"`, `"binary"`, `"lfdr"`), `setstat` (`"mean"`, `"median"`, `"maxmean"`, `"es"`,
`"wilcoxon"`, `"condfdr"`, `"globaltest"`, `"hotelling"`), `method` (`"permutation"` for the
self-contained null hypothesis, `"resampling"` for the competitive one, `"restandardization"`,
`"parametric"`) and `B`.

The output has one row per set: `set`, `size` (genes found in `X`), `statistic` (larger is more
enriched) and `p` (one-sided). With `B` draws the smallest p-value is 0, meaning below 1/`B`.

## The reproduction

The paper's simulation tables, its p53 and Hedenfalk analyses and the comparison with every
published number are in the [PMC2661051 folder](https://github.com/jeonglab-bcm/fossil/tree/main/PMC2661051)
and on the [results page](https://jeonglab-bcm.github.io/fossil/PMC2661051/).
